evidence.excerpt: When it comes to the various ways we rely on others as we engage in the pursuit of truth, testimony is paradigmatic.

Those who deny that testimony is a basic source of justification hold that testimony-based beliefs are justified only if the audience has adequate independent reasons to regard the speaker’s testimony as trustworthy.

Such a view, known as “anti-reductionism,” was defended by Thomas Reid (1764/1983), who argued that honesty (in speakers) and credulity (in audiences) are as much a part of our natural psychological endowment, and so are as worthy of being relied upon in belief-formation, as is the faculty of perception.

In addition to the question of whether testimony is a basic source of justification, a second question concerns whether we can specify the conditions on justified testimony-based belief in individualistic terms, that is, terms that are restricted to materials from the audience alone (the evidence in her possession, the reliability of her faculties, etc.).
Still, anti-individualistic views remain controversial (see Gerken 2012, Leonard 2016, 2018).
A question that has recently begun to attract more attention from social epistemologists concerns the role of technology in testimony.

sources.annotation: Surveys testimony, group belief, aggregation, networks, institutions, misleading content, and epistemic dysfunctions; empirical model results are distinguished from general prescriptions.

evidence.excerpt: A child has belief \(B\) that Hell is a real place located in the center of the earth.
There are several ways to define the terms ‘superior’, ‘inferior’, and ‘peer’ (Elga, 2007; see section 5 below).
The better one’s epistemic position, the more likely one is to be correct.

If you are convinced that a certain person is clearly lacking compared to you on many Disagreement Factors when it comes to answering the question ‘Is \(B\) true?’ then you’ll probably say that you are more likely than she is to answer the question correctly provided you are not lacking compared to her on other Disagreement Factors.
Notice that in this peer case you need not think that the two of you are equal on each Disagreement Factor.
Suppose I also believe \(P\), that Taylor is my peer regarding \(B\) in this sense: I think we are equally likely to judge \(B\) correctly.
After all, if someone asked me ‘Suppose you find out later today that Taylor sincerely thinks \(B\) is false.

But the important point here is this: if I have the view that if it turns out that she really thinks \(B\) is false then the odds that I’m right and she’s wrong are 95%, then in some sense my view is that she’s not “fully” my peer on \(B\), as I think that when it comes to the possibility of disagreement I’m very confident that I will be in the right and she won’t be.
Danny has been right, and 20% of the time they have both been wrong.

That’s very different from the global warming case in which I thought that if I were to discover that Taylor thinks \(B\) is false, the probability that I’m right and she’s wrong are 19 times the probability that I’m wrong and she’s right (95% is 19 times 5%).
But in the math case Danny thinks Janice is his likelihood peer and his conditional peer on the relevant belief.

For instance, if I am discussing with a neighbor whether our property taxes will be increasing next year, and I discover that she disagrees with me, I may have very little idea how we measure up on the Disagreement Factors.

A related question is whether there is any important difference between cases where you are justified in believing your interlocutor is your peer and cases where you may be justified in believing that your interlocutor is not your peer but lack any reason to think that you, or your interlocutor, are in the better epistemic position.
So for any two people it is quite unlikely that they are ‘weight peers’.
This is what Goldman terms the ‘novice/expert problem’ (Goldman 2001).
Evidence of the experts’ interests and biases vis-a-vis the question at issue.

evidence.excerpt: Here is a conversation that we might have: You: This plant is Pacific Poison Oak.
Broadly speaking, those working on the epistemology of authoritative testimony endorse one of two accounts: Preemptive Accounts and Non-Preemptive Accounts.

Proponents of the Preemptive Account, then, explain the difference between authoritative and non-authoritative testimony as follows: Authoritative testimony can provide you with a preemptive reason for belief, whereas non-authoritative testimony cannot.

Instead of thinking about authoritative testimony as providing preemptive reasons for belief, proponents of the Non-Preemptive Account take an authority’s testimony that p to provide a very strong reason to believe that p, where this reason is to be added to, or combined with, all of the other reasons that you have related to the proposition in question.

sources.annotation: Introduces authoritative testimony and competing preemptive and non-preemptive accounts, with objections and examples.

evidence.excerpt: Trust is an attitude we have towards people whom we hope will be trustworthy, where trustworthiness is a property not an attitude.
For most philosophers, trust is a kind of reliance although it is not mere reliance (Goldberg 2020).
Included at the end is some discussion about the nature of distrust.
One might think that if one is relying while trusting—that is, if trust is a species of reliance—then accepted vulnerability would not be essential for trust.
Annette Baier writes that “trusting can be betrayed, or at least let down, and not just disappointed” (1986: 235).

To illustrate this type of trust, consider parents who trust their teenagers with the house or the family car, believing that their [children] may well abuse their trust, but hoping by such trust to elicit, in the fullness of time, more responsible and responsive trustworthy behaviour.

sources.annotation: Distinguishes trust from reliance, justification from actual trustworthiness, and interpersonal judgment from the surrounding social climate.
